Le 17:1-16. Blood of Beasts Must Be Offered at the Tabernacle Door.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1116"/><div sID="gen1533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1116"/><hi type="bold">7. they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils--</hi>literally, "goats." The prohibition evidently alludes to the worship of the hirei-footed kind, such as Pan, Faunus, and Saturn, whose recognized symbol was a goat. This was a form of idolatry enthusiastically practised by the Egyptians, particularly in the nome or province of Mendes. Pan was supposed especially to preside over mountainous and desert regions, and it was while they were in the wilderness that the Israelites seem to have been powerfully influenced by a feeling to propitiate this idol. Moreover, the ceremonies observed in this idolatrous worship were extremely licentious and obscene, and the gross impurity of the rites gives great point and significance to the expression of Moses, "they have gone a-whoring." <div eID="gen1533" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1117"/><div sID="gen1534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1117"/><hi type="bold">8-9. Whatsoever man ... offereth ... And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle--</hi>Before the promulgation of the law, men worshipped wherever they pleased or pitched their tents. But after that event the rites of religion could be acceptably performed only at the appointed place of worship. This restriction with respect to place was necessary as a preventive of idolatry; for it prohibited the Israelites, when at a distance, from repairing to the altars of the heathen, which were commonly in groves or fields. <div eID="gen1534" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1118"/><div sID="gen1535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1118"/><hi type="bold">10. I will even set my face against that soul that eateth blood, and will cut him off from among his people--</hi>The face of God is often used in Scripture to denote His anger (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">Psa 34:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Re 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.18">Eze 38:18</reference>). The manner in which God's face would be set against such an offender was, that if the crime were public and known, he was condemned to death; if it were secret, vengeance would overtake him. (See on <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Ge 9:4</reference>). But the practice against which the law is here pointed was an idolatrous rite. The Zabians, or worshippers of the heavenly host, were accustomed, in sacrificing animals, to pour out the blood and eat a part of the flesh at the place where the blood was poured out (and sometimes the blood itself) believing that by means of it, friendship, brotherhood, and familiarity were contracted between the worshippers and the deities. They, moreover, supposed that the blood was very beneficial in obtaining for them a vision of the demon during their sleep, and a revelation of future events. The prohibition against eating blood, viewed in the light of this historic commentary and unconnected with the peculiar terms in which it is expressed, seems to have been levelled against idolatrous practices, as is still further evident from <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.25">Eze 33:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.20">1Co 10:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.21">21</reference>. <div eID="gen1535" type="x-p"/>
